title: Fresh 48 Month Inspection
notes:
Concept: Educational post explaining what a fresh 48-month inspection means to a buyer. Not tied to any aircraft — do not reference VJS inventory, a specific model, or a tail number. Evergreen, reusable.

Core idea: The 48-month is one of the big calendar-driven inspections on many business jets. It's scheduled, it's expensive, and it doesn't care how much you flew. When a listing shows one recently completed, the buyer is inheriting a clean slate instead of a bill.

Points to cover:

Calendar-based, not hours-based — it comes due whether the aircraft flew 400 hours or 40
Means real downtime at a shop, on top of the invoice
"Fresh 48-month" resets that clock for the next owner — roughly four years before it comes around again
The purchase price is only part of the number; where the aircraft sits in its inspection cycle is the other part
Two similar aircraft at similar asking prices can be very far apart in true cost depending on what's due

Takeaway: Ask where an aircraft sits in its maintenance cycle before you compare prices. It's one of the first things we look at for a client.

CTA: Talk to Vertical Jet Sales before you compare listings — we'll tell you what's actually due.

Tone: Plain and useful. Teaching, not selling. No hype.

Guardrails: Scope, cost, and interval specifics vary by aircraft type and program — keep it general. Do not state dollar figures, downtime durations, or a specific task list. Do not claim the 48-month applies to all business jets.
